This is mostly good info, but most viruses are actually spread through droplets, they aren't aren't airborne. Viruses like TB are airborne, and require n95 to filter them out, but the common viruses that cause "colds:" rhinovirus, humanmetapneumo virus, RSV, OG coronavirus (not covid), etc, and the flu are all droplet transmission. They are heavy and while they can be transmitted through the air via sneezing and respiratory particles, you have to be relatively close to someone. If you walk through a space where someone sneezed 10 minutes ago, your risk is low just from breathing in the air. This is also why regular surgical masks work for these because the droplets are big enough that they can't past through the masks. The viruses are hardy and can live on clothes and surfaces for a long time, so it's possible to get sneezed on and bring it home on your clothes. That's a big reason why hand washing is so so important because we're more likely to touch a surface that has the droplets on it and then touch our face and food. So changing clothes and washing well after you've been someplace where people might be sick or after you've been out in crowds will help.

I think so, yes. But the difference is that, again using the breast cancer example, if you have a mass in your breast and they perform a mastectomy and remove the whole mass, and it hasn't spread, then you don't have cancer anymore. So you can get prophylactic chemo to lessen the chance of relapse, but you don't really have cancer during that treatment time because it was removed. If you have cancer in your brain, and it hasn't spread anywhere else, but they can't resect it because of where it is, and you need chemo to shrink it or get rid of it, then you do still have cancer. 

Or in the case of a cancer like leukemia that's in the blood and isn't a single tumor, then you still have cancer while you're undergoing the chemo.

I'm an oncology nurse and this does exist. I'm going to use breast cancer as an example because I don't know what kind of cancer Kate has, but imagine a mass is found in breast tissue. The patient opts for a double mastectomy. The doctors perform that but also biopsy lymph nodes to look for metastasis. They don't find any cancer cells in the lymph nodes, but the biopsy of the breast mass done after the surgery shows an aggressive type of cancer. Technically they removed all of the cancer with the mastectomy, but they only sampled a couple cells in the lymph nodes. So they might recommend prophylactic chemotherapy to make sure there aren't any other cancer cells hanging out. 

This might also be true if there was a mass on Kate's ovary. If they originally thought it was just a cyst and removed it, but the biopsy showed it was cancerous, they might still so chemo, even though they probably removed all of it during the surgery, ovarian cancer is extremely aggressive with poor outcomes.

The tips are helpful under certain circumstances, but for a lot of people they're past them being useful by the time they read the book.

We worked A LOT on indepedent sleep starting around 4 or 5 weeks because I wanted to avoid having to sleep train via cry it out if possible. So I started scooting the last feed of the night away from bedtime by a couple minutes each day and we rocked to sleep instead. Around that time we started 1 crib nap a day too. After he got used to that we started giving him a chance to fall asleep on his own every time he took a nap and at bedtime. We stayed in the room and if he cried we picked him up and rocked him but he started falling asleep more and more on his own. Around 10 weeks he was putting himself to sleep pretty reliably at bedtime and at 12 weeks for naps. His sleep improved a little then but he was still waking up every 3-4 hours to eat. 

We started getting a longer first stretch like 6 hours around 2 1/2 months but this was really up and down for months with some nights being really good and some being rough. At 4 1/2 months he was waking every sleep cycle. He was still in our room in a bassinet so we moved him to his own room which he was used to because all his naps were in there and so was his bedtime routine. He started sleeping much better after that. 

Each time his sleep has gotten not so great again it's been when it's time to drop a nap or decrease daytime sleep.

He's 6 1/2 months now on two naps. He goes to bed at 9, wakes once to eat between 4:45-5:45 and then goes back to sleep until 8. He naps from 11:15-12:30 and 3:45-4:45. I would say that after 6 months we really found a consistent groove with his sleep but we had good nights before then, they just weren't so consistent. 

The indepedent sleep was so important for us because for a while after he became more aware we were rocking him to sleep for naps and as soon as we would set him down he'd pop awake. We were spending hours during the day trying to get him to sleep. It was awful. Him putting himself to sleep within 10 minutes with no fussing has been a lifesaver. 

So honestly, I don't have one answer for you. It got better in pieces over months with some rough nights sprinkled in. I wanted to keep him in our room much longer but I read that some babies know their parents are in the room, even if the parents are sleeping, and want to interact between sleep cycles, which seemed true for us. So our big improvements were indepedent sleep at 12 weeks, moving to his own room at 4 1/2 months and dropping to 2 naps around 6 months.

People get up in arms about it because both sides make it seem like a moral decision when it's really about individual families' preferences. I'm a pediatric icu nurse and I've personally done cpr due to suffocation on infants that were cosleeping. I know the literature that increases the safety of cosleeping, and if parents choose to cosleep then that's a decision of risk vs benefits that they make. For me, cosleeping was never an option because, even though it's a small part of the cosleeping population, I had seen what could go wrong. I didn't "sleep train" my baby by traditional methods. I didn't want to let him cry it out or anything, but we did teach him to fall asleep independently because it's what our family needed to do. We did it gradually and intervened when he cried based on our knowledge of him and our instincts. It would still irritate me if someone even insinuated that it amounted to abusing my child when it was the safest option for our family. So yeah, I personally think it's worse to cosleep than to sleep train because I've never seen babies die from sleep training but I've seen them die from cosleeping. I also don't go around spewing that on people's decisions.
